content: 1. Revised guidelines for Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination in infants at risk of HIV infection were published in the Weekly Epidemiological Record in 2007. These guidelines address the risks and benefits of BCG vaccination in this vulnerable population. 2. A study by Becerra MC et al., published in the Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal in 2012, examined tuberculosis (TB) in children exposed to multidrug-resistant TB at home. The findings highlighted the challenges in managing TB in such high-risk settings. 3. Azzoapardi P et al. conducted a systematic review on BCG vaccine-related disease in HIV-infected children, published in the International Journal of Tuberculosis and Lung Disease in 2009. The review emphasized the risks of disseminated BCG disease in this population. 4. Hesseling AC et al. published a consensus statement in 2008 in the International Journal of Tuberculosis and Lung Disease, discussing the revised World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations for BCG vaccination in HIV-infected infants. The statement provided clarity on the implementation of these guidelines. 5. Recommendations for investigating contacts of individuals with infectious TB in lowand middle-income countries were outlined in a 2002 publication by Rieder HL. This guidance emphasized the importance of contact tracing and preventive measures in resource-limited settings. 6. The International Standards for Tuberculosis Care, 2nd edition, published in 2009 by the Tuberculosis Coalition for Technical Assistance, provided comprehensive standards for TB diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. 7. Marais BJ et al. critically reviewed the natural history of childhood intrathoracic TB in the pre-chemotherapy era, as published in the International Journal of Tuberculosis and Lung Disease in 2004. This review offered insights into the progression and outcomes of untreated TB in children. 8. Kruk A et al. explored symptom-based screening for child TB contacts in resource-limited settings, as published in Pediatrics in 2008. The study demonstrated the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach in identifying TB cases. 9. Smieja MJ et al. reviewed the use of isoniazid for preventing TB in non-HIV-infected individuals in a Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews article from 2000. The review highlighted the efficacy of isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) in reducing TB incidence. 10. Balcells ME et al. investigated the risk of resistant TB associated with isoniazid preventive therapy in a study published in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2006. The findings underscored the importance of monitoring for drug resistance. 11. Van Halsema CL et al. examined TB outcomes and drug susceptibility in individuals exposed to isoniazid preventive therapy in high HIV prevalence settings, as published in AIDS in 2010. The study provided evidence supporting the safety and efficacy of IPT in such contexts. 12. Hill PC et al. addressed the policy-practice gap in managing child contacts of TB cases in developing countries in a PLoS Medicine article from 2011. The authors called for improved implementation of existing guidelines. 13. Munoz FM et al. studied TB among adult visitors of children with suspected TB and employees at a children's hospital, as published in Infection Control and Hospital Epidemiology in 2002. The study highlighted the risk of TB transmission in healthcare settings. 14. Cruz AT et al. conducted a similar study on TB among families of children with suspected TB and hospital employees, published in Infection Control and Hospital Epidemiology in 2011. The findings reinforced the need for stringent infection control measures. 15. WHO guidelines recommend that children living with HIV in TB-endemic settings should be regularly screened for TB at each healthcare visit. This screening aims to identify those requiring anti-TB treatment or IPT. 16. BCG vaccination is contraindicated in infants and children with known HIV infection due to the risk of disseminated BCG disease. This recommendation is detailed in WHO guidelines. 17. Symptom-based screening is recommended for children living with HIV who are close contacts of active TB cases. Those without evidence of TB disease should begin IPT regardless of age. 18. The recommended dose of isoniazid for preventive therapy is 10 mg/kg daily (range 7–15 mg/kg, maximum 300 mg/day) for at least six months. IPT does not increase the risk of isoniazid-resistant TB. 19. Children living with HIV who successfully complete TB treatment should receive an additional six months of isoniazid to prevent recurrence. 20. In high TB prevalence settings, children with suspected or confirmed pulmonary TB or tuberculous lymphadenitis should be treated with a four-drug regimen (HRZE) for two months, followed by a two-drug regimen (HR) for four months. 21. Children living with HIV have poorer responses to TB treatment compared to HIV-negative children. Risk factors for poor outcomes include severe malnutrition, co-infections, and advanced immunosuppression. 22. ART is critical in improving TB treatment outcomes in children living with HIV. Before the availability of ART, many deaths occurred within the first two months of TB treatment. 23. WHO emphasizes the integration of TB and HIV services to ensure co-infected children are identified and managed effectively. Collaborative efforts between national TB and HIV programs are essential. 24. Further research is needed to optimize TB prevention and treatment strategies for children living with HIV, particularly in resource-limited settings.
